v.why: Filling an empty input-to-output edge with a conv adds a new learnable path (e.g. +13 to +23 points in #66, #78, #223), whereas replacing an existing op on edge 3 gives only small changes.
Swapping a lossy pooling shortcut for an identity shortcut helps consistently (#23, #74, #201, #263), while replacing a conv on edge 3 with skip removes capacity and hurts (#54, #167, #181, #210).
Replacing a conv on the direct edge with parameter-free pooling loses capacity (#117, #146, #292), whereas pooling replacing none can rescue a disconnected cell (#1, #400).
Replacing the strongest conv on the first edge with pooling degrades every path through node 1 (#8, #79, #357), unlike filling an empty edge 0 (#75).
Turning the conv on node1-to-output into pooling removes learned features feeding the output (#41, #131), a bigger loss than when edge 4 was skip or none.
With no direct input-to-output edge, edge 4 may be the only path to the output, so cutting it can collapse accuracy to chance (#18).
Without the edge-3 shortcut, the output depends on node 1, so removing edge 0 can disconnect the cell (#99, #272).
When edge 0 is empty, node 2 can only be reached through edge 1, so giving edge 1 a real op restores or strengthens the main path (#14, #73, #185).
Replacing pooling on the node1-to-node2 edge with a 3x3 conv adds substantial capacity in the cell's longest path (#159, #330).
Adding a conv on a previously empty node2-to-output edge opens a new deep path to the output (#383, #392), worth more than swapping an existing op there.
